oneLiner: Up 0.73% on Friday after a weak September jobs report cut rate-hike odds; about 1% below the August 13 record close.
intro: The S&P 500 closed at 7,722.72 on Friday, October 2, up 0.73% on the day after a much weaker-than-expected September jobs report cut the odds of another Fed rate hike. Even with Friday's bounce, the index finished the week down about 0.3% and sits roughly 1% below its record close of 7,798.99 from August 13. Breadth stayed thin, with September's gains confined almost entirely to technology.

performance.heading: How the index has done
performance.body: September was a rare down month for the S&P 500, which fell 0.4% as bond yields spiked, in an otherwise strong 2026. This week it slipped about 0.3% despite Friday's 0.73% gain, leaving it roughly 1% below its August 13 record. The strip above shows the same periods on SPY, which tracks the index closely.

chart.heading: The trend against its moving averages
chart.body: On the daily chart the index has spent two weeks oscillating around its own 50-day and 200-day moving averages in the high-7,600s, rather than sitting clearly above them. That reads as a pause rather than a break: the longer-term averages are still rising, and the weekly chart further down stays above its 50- and 200-week lines.

levels.heading: Where the nearby levels sit
levels.body: The record close of 7,798.99 from August 13 is the nearest marker above, about 1% away. Below, the high-7,600s, where the daily 50- and 200-day averages sit, is the area the index has swung around for the past two weeks. The Price zones and Key levels cards show where those levels cluster on SPY today.

signals.heading: Momentum in plain words
signals.body: RSI (14) stayed in neutral territory through the week, not flagging the index as overbought or oversold even after the late-September dip and Friday's rebound. The panel above shows today's RSI and where MACD sits against its signal line on SPY.

change.heading: The weekly and monthly pattern
change.body: Close to close, September ended 0.4% lower, a rare down month this year, and this week finished about 0.3% lower even after Friday's bounce. The swings came from bond yields and jobs data rather than any change in the earnings backdrop.

marketRead: The real story this week was the labour market reversing a rate-hike scare. Through late September, sticky inflation had pushed some Fed officials toward another hike, and the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.297% on September 30, its highest level in 24 years. Friday's September jobs report flipped that: just 29,000 jobs were added against roughly 90,000 expected, and unemployment rose to 4.2%, cutting the market-implied odds of an October hike from about 64% to about 16%.

Under the surface, breadth stayed thin. Technology rose about 5% in September while financials, materials and REITs each fell around 7%, and retail investors have been net sellers for nine straight weeks even as hedge funds kept adding. The CNN Fear & Greed Index sits at 31, in Fear, a cautious reading for an index within about 1% of a record.

The bull case: the index absorbed a genuine bond-market scare without breaking its longer-term uptrend, and brokers' year-end targets are little changed, from Yardeni near 7,900 to Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan around 8,000 and UBS at 8,100. The bear case: yields are only just off a 24-year high, leadership is concentrated in a handful of AI-linked mega-caps, and Friday's relief rests on one weak jobs report that may not repeat.

That leaves two questions for the weeks ahead: whether bond yields keep easing from their late-September highs now that the labour market has cooled, and whether breadth can widen beyond technology. The August record was built on strong earnings and a resilient economy; the pullback since was driven by rates rather than profits, which is why the yield path matters more than any single headline right now.

points.label: Catalyst
points.text: September payrolls rose 29,000 against about 90,000 expected; October hike odds fell from about 64% to about 16%.

points.label: Breadth
points.text: September's gains were mostly technology (about +5%); financials, materials and REITs fell around 7% each.

points.label: Rates
points.text: The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.297% on September 30, a 24-year high, before easing after the jobs data.

breadth.source: Not in the 4 Oct weekly update

watchDown: The index closes a full week below its daily 200-day moving average, rather than swinging around it as it has for two weeks.
The 10-year Treasury yield climbs back above its late-September high near 5.3%.
Breadth narrows further from September's technology-only gains, or the Fear & Greed Index slides deeper into fear.
The soft jobs data proves a one-off, reviving the rate-hike concerns behind September's bond-market slide.
watchUp: The index clears its record close of 7,798.99 and moves toward the 7,900–8,100 range of year-end targets.
The 10-year yield keeps easing from its 24-year high, taking pressure off valuations.
Financials, materials and REITs stabilise and breadth widens beyond technology.
The nine-week run of net retail outflows ends and participation in the rally broadens.
